analysis.one_liner: Bans senior executive branch officials from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and never got a committee vote; it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit the President, Vice President, top executive branch employees, senior military officers, and their spouses from holding or trading individual stocks and similar investments, except through a qualified blind trust or diversified funds. Any profits from violations would be forfeited to the Treasury, and the Attorney General could impose fines up to $10,000 or the amount of the improper gain. Government auditors would check compliance annually.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who want government decisions made without officials personally profiting from stock tied to those decisions. The bill also protects covered officials who comply, by giving them a 180-day window to sell and allowing blind trusts.

how_it_helps.text: Bans covered officials and their spouses from holding, buying, or selling individual stocks, security futures, commodities, and similar instruments while in office [S2][S3].
Requires any profit from a violating transaction to be disgorged to the Treasury, and allows civil fines of up to $10,000 or the amount received, whichever is greater [S3].
Requires the Government Accountability Office to audit compliance of a representative sample of covered officials annually and report to the ethics committees [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Senior executive branch officials, senior military officers, and their spouses, who would have to sell individual stocks within 180 days of taking office or place them in a blind trust.

drawbacks.text: The civil penalty is capped at $10,000 or the amount of the improper gain, which a supporter would acknowledge is modest enforcement compared with some earlier proposals for congressional trading bans [S3].

The bill gives current officials a 180-day grace period to sell and exempts holdings in a qualified blind trust, so substantial wealth can still remain invested in markets the official's policies influence [S3].

Critics of such bans argue that forcing senior officials and officers to divest may deter qualified people from government service, though the bill's blind trust and diversified-fund exceptions are designed to answer that concern [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — preventing senior officials from personally trading stocks their decisions can move — addresses a real conflict of interest, and the exceptions for blind trusts and diversified funds keep the burden reasonable. The main weakness is soft enforcement: civil fines are modest and compliance rests on audits of a sample of officials rather than every official, so a determined violator might face limited consequences.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced the bill on March 7, 2023 [S1][S2].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day, which was its last recorded action [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the committee or the Senate taking any further action on the bill [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Senior executive branch officials and their spouses keep the ability to hold and trade individual stocks while in office, and no new disclosure or audit requirements took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Senior officials, whose trading was untouched

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or floor action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsor with no cosponsors from either party and no votes make it impossible to read a party split from the record [S4].

industries.industry: Senior executive branch officials and their spouses
industries.note: The bill would force them to divest individual stocks or use blind trusts, ending their ability to personally profit from stock moves tied to government decisions. Their interest in keeping that ability runs against the public's interest in decisions made without personal financial stakes.
